readings.focus: Inspiration, slow craft, and a poet’s fear that his gift has gone.
readings.context: Addressed to Robert Bridges, Hopkins’s friend, who later edited this 1918 volume. It was written in April 1889, weeks before Hopkins died. The muse is poetic inspiration; the grave accent in “quenchèd” marks a sounded syllable; “want” in line 10 means lack.

excerpt.locator: To R. B. (poem 51); complete individual work; opens “THE fine delight that fathers thought; the strong Spur, live and lancing like the…”; closes “…that scarcely breathes that bliss Now, yields you, with some sighs, our explanation.”.

questions.prompt: Follow the metaphor in the octave. How is making a poem like conceiving and bearing a child?
facilitatorNotes: Inspiration is the father: a flame that breathes once and goes out, leaving the mind “a mother of immortal song.” She carries the poem nine months, even nine years, shaping it; a “widow” of the lost insight, she works on with sure aim and hand.
evidence: Leaves yet the mind a mother of immortal song.
Nine months she then, nay years, nine years she long Within her wears, bears, cares and moulds the same:
The widow of an insight lost she lives,

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say he lacks, and how does he explain it to his friend?
facilitatorNotes: He lacks “the one rapture of an inspiration.” If his lines miss the roll and rise of song, his “winter world,” barely breathing, is the explanation he offers, with sighs.
evidence: I want the one rapture of an inspiration.
My winter world, that scarcely breathes that bliss

questions.prompt: Is the sonnet itself evidence for or against its claim that inspiration has failed?
facilitatorNotes: Its control and music (the list “the roll, the rise, the carol, the creation”) seem to contradict the complaint. Or the poem shows the octave’s other kind of making, years of patient moulding without the first rapture. Either answer can be argued from the text.
evidence: The roll, the rise, the carol, the creation,

readings.title: The Wreck of the Deutschland: Part the First
readings.challenge: Read each stanza aloud before you think about it, and mark the words that make a spiritual crisis feel like a bodily one.
readings.focus: A man’s own struggle with a God of terror and of love, told before the poem turns to the shipwreck.
readings.context: The Wreck of the Deutschland is Hopkins’s longest poem; the stanza numbers are his. The dedication names five nuns exiled from Germany by the Falk Laws, Prussian laws of the 1870s against the Catholic Church, who drowned when the Deutschland, a German emigrant ship, ran aground off the English coast. Part the Second, a later night, tells the wreck; Part the First, tonight, is about the poet himself. The Host is the consecrated bread of the Mass; a voel is a bare hill (a Welsh word); instressed is Hopkins’s coinage for an inner pressure of being, felt and grasped; a sloe is a wild plum; Paul was converted in a moment on the road to Damascus, Austin (St Augustine) slowly over years.

excerpt.locator: The Wreck of the Deutschland (poem 4), the dedication and Part the First, stanzas 1 to 10; opens “ To the happy memory of five Franciscan Nuns exiles by the Falk Laws drowned between…”; closes “…skill, Make mércy in all of us, out of us all Mastery, but be adored, but be adored King.”.

questions.prompt: Stanza 1 says God “bound bones and veins in me” and then “almost unmade” him. What experience do stanzas 1 to 3 describe, and which words make it physical?
facilitatorNotes: An experience of terror before God that ends in consent: he “did say yes” under “lightning and lashed rod.” The crisis is felt in the body: a heart that swoons, a “midriff astrain,” a “horror of height.” Caught between God’s frown and the “hurtle of hell,” he flees to “the heart of the Host,” to Christ in the sacrament. The physical words keep the experience from sounding like doctrine.
evidence: Thou hast bound bones and veins in me, fastened me flesh,
I did say yes O at lightning and lashed rod;
And fled with a fling of the heart to the heart of the Host.

questions.prompt: Stanza 4 compares the speaker to sand in an hourglass and to water in a well. How do the two images differ, and what holds him steady?
facilitatorNotes: The sand looks firm at the glass wall but is “mined with a motion,” always slipping toward the fall: a life running out. The water in a well is calm, “to a poise, to a pane,” because a vein from the hills keeps feeding it. What steadies him comes from outside, “Christ’s gift,” like a spring. Some readers hear both images as true at once: he is draining and replenished.
evidence: I am soft sift In an hourglass
I steady as a water in a well, to a poise, to a pane,
a vein Of the gospel proffer, a pressure, a principle, Christ's gift.

questions.prompt: Stanzas 6 to 8 say that the “stress” people feel comes neither “out of his bliss” nor “first from heaven.” Where does it come from, and what does the image of the sloe add?
facilitatorNotes: It comes from Christ’s life on earth and his Passion (“It dates from day Of his going in Galilee”), which “rides time like riding a river” and reaches each person at the moment the heart is “hard at bay.” The sloe bitten till it bursts is that moment: the whole being floods, “sour or sweet,” and people come to Christ whether they mean it or not. Readers may take the sloe as conversion, or as any crisis that shows what a person is.
evidence: Not out of his bliss Springs the stress felt
It dates from day Of his going in Galilee;
How a lush-kept plush-capped sloe Will, mouthed to flesh-burst, Gush!

questions.prompt: In stanzas 9 and 10 the speaker offers God two ways of mastering people. What are they, and why might Part the First end with this prayer before a poem about a shipwreck?
facilitatorNotes: Sudden and violent, with anvil and fire, “as once at a crash Paul,” or slow and gentle, “stealing as Spring,” as with Augustine. God is “lightning and love,” “a winter and warm.” He asks God to wring “Man’s malice, with wrecking and storm”: the wreck to come will be read as one of those ways. Readers may find the prayer moving or troubling, since it welcomes a storm.
evidence: Wring thy rebel, dogged in den, Man's malice, with wrecking and storm.
Thou art lightning and love, I found it, a winter and warm;
Whether at once, as once at a crash Paul, Or as Austin, a lingering-out sweet skill,

readings.title: The Blessed Virgin compared to the Air we Breathe
readings.challenge: Follow the one comparison through the whole poem: list everything air does, and what each thing becomes when it is said of Mary.
readings.focus: Devotion worked out as an argument from the physical world, from breathing to the colour of the sky.
readings.context: Hopkins was a Catholic priest, and this is a poem of devotion to Mary, the mother of Jesus; you need not share the faith to follow its argument. Mary Immaculate names the Catholic teaching that Mary was conceived without sin. Frailest-flixed means of the finest down; riddles means sifts through; an almoner gives alms on another’s behalf; ghostly means spiritual; Bethlem is Bethlehem; azurèd means made blue; the seven or seven times seven hued sunbeam is white light holding every colour; quartz-fret is glittering crystal; the daystar is the sun; froward means wilful.

excerpt.locator: The Blessed Virgin compared to the Air we Breathe (poem 37); complete individual work; opens “WILD air, world-mothering air, Nestling me everywhere, That each eyelash or hair Girdles;…”; closes “…air, air wild, Wound with thee, in thee isled, Fold home, fast fold thy child.”.

questions.prompt: List what air does in the opening lines. Which qualities of air does Hopkins choose, and why do they suit what he will say of Mary?
facilitatorNotes: Air is everywhere and intimate (it girdles “each eyelash or hair”), sustains life more than food does, is “never spent,” and is a “nursing element.” Each quality prepares a claim about Mary’s grace: present to everyone, constant, mothering. The rhymed three-stress lines, quick as breathing, keep the comparison light.
evidence: WILD air, world-mothering air, Nestling me everywhere,
My more than meat and drink, My meal at every wink;
This needful, never spent, And nursing element;

questions.prompt: Hopkins calls Mary “Merely a woman” whose power is “Great as no goddess’s.” How does the poem keep her from becoming a goddess?
facilitatorNotes: Her one work is to let God’s glory through, “Through her and from her flow Off, and no way but so”: like air, she is a medium. Later he insists her part is “no part but what will Be Christ our Saviour still.” Her greatness is her transparency, which is the poem’s way of honouring her without rivalling God.
evidence: Merely a woman, yet Whose presence, power is Great as no goddess's
This one work has to do-- Let all God's glory through,
Yet no part but what will Be Christ our Saviour still.

questions.prompt: The longest comparison is the blue sky. What would the sun look like without air, and what does that say about seeing God through Mary?
facilitatorNotes: Air makes the sky blue yet “does no prejudice” to light: every colour still shows. Without it the sun would be “A blear and blinding ball With blackness bound,” the stars flecks of coal. God’s glory “bare would blind”; through Mary it is “Made sweeter, not made dim” and “Sifted to suit our sight.” Mediation here is a kindness to human eyes, not a barrier.
evidence: Stain light. Yea, mark you this: It does no prejudice.
A blear and blinding ball With blackness bound,
And her hand leaves his light Sifted to suit our sight.

questions.prompt: What do “New Nazareths in us” and “New Bethlems” do to the story of Christ’s birth? How does the ending return to the beginning?
facilitatorNotes: The birth happens again in each believer, “morning, noon, and eve,” making “New self and nobler me.” The last stanza asks Mary to be his “atmosphere” and closes on the opening’s “World-mothering air,” now folded round him like a child. Readers outside the faith can still read it as a poem about what surrounds a self and makes it new.
evidence: New Nazareths in us, Where she shall yet conceive Him,
Be thou then, O thou dear Mother, my atmosphere;
World-mothering air, air wild, Wound with thee, in thee isled, Fold home, fast fold thy child.
